text: Every API server request answers two questions. Authentication asks who you are. Authorization — RBAC — asks whether that identity may do this specific thing. RBAC only grants, never denies explicitly, so a request matching no rule is denied by default. That's the model behind every Role, RoleBinding, and ServiceAccount in this lesson.

A Role is the namespaced version — its rules only ever apply inside the namespace it's created in. The grammar is three fields: apiGroups, resources, and verbs. This pod-reader Role lives in the payments namespace and grants get, list, and watch on pods and pod logs — read-only, and nothing outside that one namespace, no matter how the binding gets written later.

A ClusterRole drops the namespace entirely: it grants permission on cluster-scoped resources like nodes, or defines a reusable rule set bound per-namespace later. Kubernetes ships built-in ones worth knowing — view, edit, admin, and cluster-admin, which is really just a rule matching every verb, every resource, every API group. Binding is where the real decision happens: a RoleBinding scopes a grant to one namespace even if it references a ClusterRole; a ClusterRoleBinding makes it apply everywhere — exactly how cluster-admin ends up handed out by accident.

A ServiceAccount is the identity a Pod presents to the API server, not a human user. Every namespace gets a default ServiceAccount, and every Pod that doesn't name one uses it — so a whole cluster of workloads can end up sharing one identity, making it impossible to tell which app did what. Create a dedicated ServiceAccount per workload instead, bound only to the Role it needs. Since Kubernetes 1.22, mounted tokens come from the TokenRequest API by default: short-lived, audience-bound, and auto-rotated — a real step up from the old tokens that sat in a Secret indefinitely.

Don't guess what a binding actually grants — ask the API server directly. kubectl auth can-i, with a verb, a resource, and an --as flag naming the ServiceAccount, returns a plain yes or no from the real authorizer. Add --list and it dumps every permission that identity holds, which is the fastest way to audit a Role someone else wrote before it ships, or to sanity-check your own.

Four objects, two jobs: Roles and ClusterRoles define what's allowed, RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings decide how far that grant reaches. Get comfortable with that split, because next lesson builds on identity in a different direction — not who a Pod is, but what it's allowed to do once it's actually running, through Pod Security Standards.
